input.command:

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

df = pd.read_csv('artifacts/_project/supplement/data/features_all_models.csv')

features = ['entropy_mean', 'entropy_std', 'entropy_min', 'entropy_max', 'tail_decay', 'ttr', 'hapax_ratio']
feature_labels = ['Entropy Mean', 'Entropy Std', 'Entropy Min', 'Entropy Max', 'Tail Decay', 'TTR', 'Hapax Ratio']

# Categorize features
drifting = ['entropy_mean', 'ttr', 'hapax_ratio']
intermediate = ['entropy_std', 'entropy_min']
stationary = ['entropy_max', 'tail_decay']

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(11, 9))
axes_flat = axes.flatten()

depths = sorted(df['depth'].unique())
generators = sorted(df['model_name'].unique())

# Colors for generators (Okabe-Ito)
gen_colors = ['#E69F00', '#56B4E9', '#009E73', '#F0E442', '#0072B2', '#D55E00', '#CC79A7', '#999999']

for i, (feat, label) in enumerate(zip(features, feature_labels)):
    ax = axes_flat[i]
    
    # Plot per-generator thin lines
    for j, gen in enumerate(generators):
        gen_df = df[df['model_name'] == gen]
        means = gen_df.groupby('depth')[feat].mean()
        ax.plot(means.index, means.values, '-', color=gen_colors[j], alpha=0.3, linewidth=0.8)
    
    # Plot overall mean ± std (bold)
    overall_means = df.groupby('depth')[feat].mean()
    overall_stds = df.groupby('depth')[feat].std()
    
    ax.plot(depths, overall_means.values, 'k-', linewidth=2.0, zorder=5)
    ax.fill_between(depths, 
                    (overall_means - overall_stds).values,
                    (overall_means + overall_stds).values,
                    alpha=0.15, color='black', zorder=4)
    
    # Add regression line + stats
    rho, pval = stats.spearmanr(df['depth'], df[feat])
    slope, intercept, r_value, _, _ = stats.linregress(depths, overall_means.values)
    
    # Color-code title by category
    if feat in drifting:
        title_color = '#D55E00'
        cat = 'DRIFTING'
    elif feat in stationary:
        title_color = '#009E73'
        cat = 'STATIONARY'
    else:
        title_color = '#0072B2'
        cat = 'INTERMEDIATE'
    
    ax.set_title(f'{label} [{cat}]', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold', color=title_color)
    ax.set_xlabel('Depth', fontsize=9)
    ax.set_ylabel(label, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xticks(depths)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
    
    # Annotation box
    ax.text(0.98, 0.05, f'ρ = {rho:.3f}\nR² = {r_value**2:.3f}', 
            transform=ax.transAxes, ha='right', va='bottom', fontsize=8,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.3', facecolor='lightyellow', edgecolor='gray', alpha=0.9))

# Remove last 2 empty subplots
axes_flat[7].set_visible(False)
axes_flat[8].set_visible(False)

# Legend for generators
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
legend_elements = [Line2D([0], [0], color=gen_colors[j], linewidth=1, alpha=0.5, label=gen) 
                   for j, gen in enumerate(generators)]
legend_elements.append(Line2D([0], [0], color='black', linewidth=2, label='Mean (all gen.)'))
axes_flat[8].set_visible(True)
axes_flat[8].axis('off')
axes_flat[8].legend(handles=legend_elements, loc='center', fontsize=8, ncol=2, frameon=True)

plt.tight_layout(pad=1.5)
plt.savefig('docs/chart/fig_appendix_ddr_trends.pdf', bbox_inches='tight', dpi=300)
plt.savefig('artifacts/_project/chart/fig_appendix_ddr_trends.pdf', bbox_inches='tight', dpi=300)
print("Created fig_appendix_ddr_trends.pdf")
EOF

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import umap

df = pd.read_csv('artifacts/_project/supplement/data/features_all_models.csv')
features = ['entropy_mean', 'entropy_std', 'entropy_min', 'entropy_max', 'tail_decay', 'ttr', 'hapax_ratio']

# Subsample for UMAP (use stratified sample: 1000 per depth)
np.random.seed(42)
sampled = df.groupby('depth').apply(lambda x: x.sample(min(1500, len(x)), random_state=42)).reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Using {len(sampled)} samples for UMAP")

X = sampled[features].values
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)

# Run UMAP
reducer = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=30, min_dist=0.3, random_state=42, n_components=2)
embedding = reducer.fit_transform(X_scaled)
print("UMAP complete")

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5))

# Left: colored by depth
ax = axes[0]
depth_colors = {0: '#009E73', 1: '#0072B2', 2: '#D55E00', 3: '#CC79A7', 4: '#F0E442'}
for d in sorted(sampled['depth'].unique()):
    mask = sampled['depth'].values == d
    ax.scatter(embedding[mask, 0], embedding[mask, 1], 
              c=depth_colors[d], s=5, alpha=0.4, label=f'Depth {d}', rasterized=True)
ax.set_xlabel('UMAP-1', fontsize=10)
ax.set_ylabel('UMAP-2', fontsize=10)
ax.set_title('(a) UMAP by Generation Depth', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
ax.legend(fontsize=8, markerscale=3, loc='upper right')
ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)

# Right: colored by binary (gen-0 vs gen-1 vs gen-2+)
ax = axes[1]
binary_colors = {0: '#009E73', 1: '#0072B2'}  # 0=gen-0, 1=gen-1+
binary_labels = np.where(sampled['depth'].values == 0, 0, 
                         np.where(sampled['depth'].values == 1, 1, 2))
triclass_colors = {0: '#009E73', 1: '#0072B2', 2: '#D55E00'}
triclass_names = {0: 'gen-0 (human)', 1: 'gen-1', 2: 'gen-2+'}
for c in [0, 1, 2]:
    mask = binary_labels == c
    ax.scatter(embedding[mask, 0], embedding[mask, 1],
              c=triclass_colors[c], s=5, alpha=0.4, label=triclass_names[c], rasterized=True)
ax.set_xlabel('UMAP-1', fontsize=10)
ax.set_ylabel('UMAP-2', fontsize=10)
ax.set_title('(b) UMAP by 3-Class Label', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
ax.legend(fontsize=8, markerscale=3, loc='upper right')
ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)

plt.tight_layout(pad=1.5)
plt.savefig('docs/chart/fig_appendix_umap.pdf', bbox_inches='tight', dpi=300)
plt.savefig('artifacts/_project/chart/fig_appendix_umap.pdf', bbox_inches='tight', dpi=300)
print("Created fig_appendix_umap.pdf")
EOF

    ax.scatter(embedding[mask, 0], embedding[mask, 1], 
              c=depth_colors[d], s=5, alpha=0.4, label=f'Depth {d}', rasterized=True)

Two concurrent works are most directly relevant.
\citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, showing progressive information loss.
\citet{markovian_chains} demonstrate that semantic-preservation constraints induce attractor dynamics bounding distinguishable depth to approximately three classes; their analysis focuses on characterizing convergence behavior through model-based perplexity tracking.
We differ in three respects: (i) we study \emph{non-paraphrastic continuation} chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal; (ii) we use handcrafted features rather than model-internal representations, enabling the DDR decomposition into drifting vs.\ stationary components; and (iii) we focus on \emph{estimating} depth from text rather than characterizing the convergence dynamics of the generation process.

\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
\label{sec:related-diversity}

Declining lexical diversity in LLM-generated text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment \cite{writing_diversity} settings.

Under 10-fold stratified CV, the full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.773) significantly outperforms surface-only (F1\,=\,0.688) and reference-only (F1\,=\,0.713; McNemar $p \approx 0$; Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
Reference-only features yield higher binary F1 (0.833 vs.\ 0.695 for the full ensemble) because surface lexical features introduce noise at the gen-1/gen-2+ boundary.
However, surface features are essential for 3-class classification, where they improve gen-0 discrimination by capturing vocabulary diversity patterns absent in reference-model entropy statistics (Full 3-class F1\,=\,0.773 vs.\ Reference-only 0.713).
Permutation importance: hapax ratio (0.35), entropy mean (0.23), TTR (0.18).
Leave-one-feature-out confirms 6 of 7 features contribute positively (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
Alternative references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) achieve comparable LOGO F1 (spread 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}), with consistently negative entropy drift, confirming DDR is a property of recursive generation.

\paragraph{Temperature robustness.}
Depth signal is robust across $t = 0.5$--$0.9$ (F1 within 1\,pp of the default $t{=}0.7$) but degrades ${\sim}6$\,pp at $t{=}1.0$ (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), where sampling randomness overwhelms the systematic location shift.

We differ in three respects: (i) we study \emph{non-paraphrastic continuation} chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal; (ii) we use handcrafted features rather than model-internal representations, enabling the DDR decomposition into drifting vs.\ stationary components; and (iii) we focus on \emph{estimating} depth from text rather than characterizing the convergence dynamics of the generation process.

That both works independently converge on approximately three distinguishable classes reflects different mechanisms reaching the same practical ceiling.
\citet{markovian_chains} derive this bound from Markovian attractor dynamics: semantic-preservation constraints create fixed points where successive outputs become indistinguishable under model-internal perplexity.
We observe the same bound empirically through feature-space compression: inter-class KS statistics drop sharply after depth 2 (gen-1$\rightarrow$gen-2: KS\,=\,0.28 vs.\ gen-2$\rightarrow$gen-3: KS\,=\,0.09 for entropy mean), collapsing discriminative margins.
The approaches are complementary: their theoretical framework explains \emph{why} convergence occurs (attractor dynamics in semantic space), while our DDR decomposition reveals \emph{what} converges (location properties) versus what remains stable (distributional shape), providing an empirical signature that can be exploited for detection without access to model internals.

问题：
- KS 值都是近似值，不精确

- tail_decay: KS=0.052, p_corrected=3.1×10⁻⁹ (SIGNIFICANT)
- entropy_std: KS=0.285 (intermediate)

```
drifting features exhibit large distributional shifts between gen-1 and gen-2+ (entropy mean KS\,=\,0.537, TTR\,=\,0.517, hapax ratio\,=\,0.516; all $p \approx 0$), while shape features show order-of-magnitude smaller shifts (entropy max KS\,=\,0.043, tail decay\,=\,0.052).

```

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

\paragraph{Equivalence testing.}
We apply a two one-sided $t$-test (TOST) with a $\pm$2\% relative margin (equivalence bounds $\pm$0.047 on the ppl scale) to formally assess whether the depth-aware and random subsampling conditions produce practically indistinguishable perplexity.
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951): size-matched (random) ppl\,=\,2.367 vs.\ depth 0--1 ppl\,=\,2.387, $\Delta$\,=\,0.020.
TOST confirms equivalence ($p = 1.1 \times 10^{-4}$), indicating the two curation strategies yield practically indistinguishable downstream quality within the $\pm$2\% margin.
Cross-seed standard deviation is below 0.001 for both variants.

Comparing the full dataset ($n$\,=\,12{,}299, ppl\,=\,2.335) against the depth-filtered subset ($n$\,=\,3{,}951, ppl\,=\,2.387): TOST \emph{rejects} equivalence (minimum equivalence margin\,=\,0.053, exceeding the $\pm$2\% bound), confirming that data quantity drives perplexity reduction beyond what depth-aware selection can recover.

Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training; at fixed sample count, depth-aware curation is statistically equivalent to uninformed random subsampling.

\subsection*{Margin Sensitivity Analysis}

To assess the robustness of the equivalence conclusion to margin choice, we repeat the TOST procedure across multiple equivalence margins \cite{lakens_equivalence}, following the recommendation to report sensitivity across plausible bounds rather than relying on a single threshold (Table~\ref{tab:tost-margins}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Comparison} & \textbf{Margin} & \textbf{Equiv?} & \textbf{TOST $p$} \\
\midrule

                                        & $\pm$2\% & Yes & $1 \times 10^{-6}$ \\
                                        & $\pm$3\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
                                        & $\pm$5\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
\midrule
Full (12{,}299) vs.\ Depth 0--1 (3{,}951) & $\pm$1\% & No & 1.0 \\
                                            & $\pm$2\% & No & 1.0 \\
                                            & $\pm$3\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
                                            & $\pm$5\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{TOST equivalence testing across multiple margins. ``Equiv?'' indicates whether equivalence is established at $\alpha = 0.05$.}
\label{tab:tost-margins}

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

\paragraph{Equivalence testing.}
We apply a two one-sided $t$-test (TOST) with a $\pm$2\% relative margin (equivalence bounds $\pm$0.047 on the ppl scale) to formally assess whether the depth-aware and random subsampling conditions produce practically indistinguishable perplexity.
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951): size-matched (random) ppl\,=\,2.367 vs.\ depth 0--1 ppl\,=\,2.387, $\Delta$\,=\,0.020.
TOST confirms equivalence ($p = 1.1 \times 10^{-4}$), indicating the two curation strategies yield practically indistinguishable downstream quality within the $\pm$2\% margin.
Cross-seed standard deviation is below 0.001 for both variants.

Comparing the full dataset ($n$\,=\,12{,}299, ppl\,=\,2.335) against the depth-filtered subset ($n$\,=\,3{,}951, ppl\,=\,2.387): TOST \emph{rejects} equivalence (minimum equivalence margin\,=\,0.053, exceeding the $\pm$2\% bound), confirming that data quantity drives perplexity reduction beyond what depth-aware selection can recover.

Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training; at fixed sample count, depth-aware curation is statistically equivalent to uninformed random subsampling.

Can depth-aware data curation improve downstream language model quality?
We fine-tune OLMo-2-0425-1B on five data variants (3 seeds each) and evaluate perplexity on a held-out test set (Table~\ref{tab:downstream}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrc}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Test PPL} \\
\midrule
All depths            & 12{,}299 & 2.335 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Size-matched (random) & 3{,}951  & 2.367 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0--1 only       & 3{,}951  & 2.387 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
Binary-filtered       & 3{,}951  & 2.389 $\pm$ 0.000 \\
Depth 0 only          & 797      & 2.681 $\pm$ 0.001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream fine-tuning perplexity (OLMo-2-0425-1B, mean $\pm$ std across 3 seeds). At equal sample count, random subsampling (2.367) outperforms depth-aware curation (depth 0--1: 2.387, binary-filtered: 2.389).}
\label{tab:downstream}
\end{table}

The results are unambiguous: data quantity dominates depth composition.
Training on all 12{,}299 samples yields the lowest perplexity (2.335).
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951), random subsampling (2.367) \emph{outperforms} both depth-stratified selection (depth 0--1: 2.387) and binary detection filtering (2.389).
Cross-seed variance is below 0.002 across all variants, confirming the robustness of this null result.

Restricting training to human-only text (depth 0, $n$\,=\,797) produces a sharp perplexity increase to 2.681, driven primarily by the 5$\times$ reduction in data volume rather than depth composition per se.

\paragraph{Equivalence testing.}
We apply a two one-sided $t$-test (TOST) with a $\pm$2\% relative margin (equivalence bounds $\pm$0.047 on the ppl scale) to formally assess whether the depth-aware and random subsampling conditions produce practically indistinguishable perplexity.
At equal sample count ($n$\,=\,3{,}951): size-matched (random) ppl\,=\,2.367 vs.\ depth 0--1 ppl\,=\,2.387, $\Delta$\,=\,0.020.
TOST confirms equivalence ($p = 1.1 \times 10^{-4}$), indicating the two curation strategies yield practically indistinguishable downstream quality within the $\pm$2\% margin.
Cross-seed standard deviation is below 0.001 for both variants.

Comparing the full dataset ($n$\,=\,12{,}299, ppl\,=\,2.335) against the depth-filtered subset ($n$\,=\,3{,}951, ppl\,=\,2.387): TOST \emph{rejects} equivalence (minimum equivalence margin\,=\,0.053, exceeding the $\pm$2\% bound), confirming that data quantity drives perplexity reduction beyond what depth-aware selection can recover.

Knowing the generation depth of a document does not, by itself, make it more or less useful for training; at fixed sample count, depth-aware curation is statistically equivalent to uninformed random subsampling.

\subsection*{Margin Sensitivity Analysis}

To assess the robustness of the equivalence conclusion to margin choice, we repeat the TOST procedure across multiple equivalence margins \cite{lakens_equivalence}, following the recommendation to report sensitivity across plausible bounds rather than relying on a single threshold (Table~\ref{tab:tost-margins}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Comparison} & \textbf{Margin} & \textbf{Equiv?} & \textbf{TOST $p$} \\
\midrule
Full (12{,}299) vs.\ Random (3{,}951) & $\pm$1\% & No & 1.0 \\
                                        & $\pm$2\% & Yes & $1 \times 10^{-6}$ \\
                                        & $\pm$3\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
                                        & $\pm$5\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
\midrule
Full (12{,}299) vs.\ Depth 0--1 (3{,}951) & $\pm$1\% & No & 1.0 \\
                                            & $\pm$2\% & No & 1.0 \\
                                            & $\pm$3\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
                                            & $\pm$5\% & Yes & $< 10^{-10}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{TOST equivalence testing across multiple margins. ``Equiv?'' indicates whether equivalence is established at $\alpha = 0.05$.}
\label{tab:tost-margins}
\end{table}

The full dataset vs.\ random subsample comparison passes equivalence at the $\pm$2\% margin ($p = 10^{-6}$), while the full vs.\ depth 0--1 comparison requires a $\pm$3\% margin.
In absolute terms, perplexity differences are small: $\Delta$\,=\,0.032 (full vs.\ random, 1.4\% of baseline) and $\Delta$\,=\,0.052 (full vs.\ depth 0--1, 2.2\% of baseline).

Cohen's $d$ values are 86.0 (full vs.\ random) and 119.7 (full vs.\ depth 0--1).
These appear large but are unreliable: with only $n$\,=\,3 seeds per condition, the pooled standard deviation is extremely small ($<$0.001), artificially inflating $d$.
The inflated effect sizes reflect low seed-level variance (confirming reproducibility) rather than practically meaningful perplexity differences.
The TOST framework with pre-specified relative margins provides a more appropriate assessment than Cohen's $d$ in this low-seed regime.
